sentences.text: Romerodus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, a group of cartilaginous fish that includes modern sharks and rays, but it is now classified specifically as a holocephalan, a lineage represented today only by chimaeras.
This genus is placed within the family Caseodontidae.
Most of its skeleton was made of cartilage that had been calcified, with the exception of the vertebral centra and the dorsal fin radials.
A single dorsal fin was supported by fused basal cartilage and positioned above the pectoral girdle.
The animal possessed broad, flattened, overlapping teeth that resembled pavement stones.
Uniquely, Romerodus had a whorl of teeth arranged along the midline of its lower jaw.
This tooth whorl on the lower jaw accounted for approximately 25% of the skull's total length.
The largest known Romerodus reached approximately 50 cm in total length.
However, a specimen of an indeterminate species in the René Kindlimann collection measures 56 cm in length.
A life-sized replica of Helicoprion davidsii displayed at the Idaho Museum of Natural History used the body proportions and anatomy of caseodonts like Romerodus as a model.
The genus Romerodus was named and described by Rainer Zangerl in 1981.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is the incomplete articulated fossil FMNH PF 8522 from the Stark Shale.
Zangerl described the species from multiple crushed but well-preserved body fossils.
All described Romerodus specimens come from the Hansen Quarry in Sarpy County, Nebraska.
The only named species, R. orodontus, was found in organic shale deposits in Nebraska, USA.
Isolated teeth possibly belonging to Romerodus have also been found in the Early Permian Phosphoria Formation in Grand Teton and Yellowstone national parks.
Romerodus is considered an active, nektonic carnivore and a very powerful swimmer.
It lived in deep marine waters and was adapted as a pelagic carnivore.

Scaling Romerodus's proportions suggests the largest Helicoprion individuals may have reached 7 to 11 meters in length, though this estimate depends on the assumption that both species shared similar ecology and phylogeny.
The type species of the genus Romerodus is Romerodus orodontus.
Romerodus lived during the Kasimovian stage, between 307 and 303.7 million years ago.
Fossils date to the Pennsylvanian subperiod and possibly the Early Permian.
The animal lived during the Carboniferous and possibly the Permian periods in North America.
During the Late Carboniferous, the area now known as Nebraska was part of the Late Pennsylvanian Midcontinent Sea, a deep inland sea rich in phosphates and organic material.
Fossils from the type specimen were found in the Stark Shale, which was a marine depositional environment.
It is debated whether eugeneodonts' shark-like morphology was due to shared ecology rather than direct ancestry with sharks.
